name: Goode 2011
aliases: Behavioral therapy for persistent postprostatectomy incontinence
question: Does behavioral therapy reduce persistent incontinence after radical prostatectomy, and do biofeedback and electrical stimulation add benefit?

design.blinding: Participants and treating clinicians unblinded; diary scorers blinded

arms.label: behavioral therapy plus biofeedback and pelvic floor electrical stimulation

design.population: Community-dwelling men aged 51–84 years with incontinence persisting 1–17 years after radical prostatectomy, enrolled at one university and two Veterans Affairs continence clinics.
design.description: Three-site, assessor-blinded, three-arm randomized superiority trial

verdictNote: Both active programs beat delayed treatment; biofeedback and stimulation added no demonstrated benefit.
takeaway: Eight weeks of behavioral therapy reduced weekly incontinence episodes more than delayed treatment in men with persistent postprostatectomy incontinence; adding biofeedback and pelvic floor electrical stimulation did not improve the reduction.

reports.label: Initial and 12-month follow-up report
reports.citation: Goode PS, Burgio KL, Johnson TM 2nd, et al. "Behavioral Therapy With or Without Biofeedback and Pelvic Floor Electrical Stimulation for Persistent Postprostatectomy Incontinence: A Randomized Controlled Trial." *JAMA.* 2011;305(2):151-159. doi:10.1001/jama.2010.1972
reports.followUp: Primary endpoint at 8 weeks; active arms followed to 12 months after treatment (81 with diary outcome at 12 months)
reports.followUpLocator: Full text, Methods: Treatment Durability; Results; Table 3

results.measure: Mean percent reduction from baseline on 7-day bladder diary at 8 weeks; effect is percentage-point difference, behavioral therapy minus delayed treatment
results.note: Omnibus P = .001; prespecified pairwise alpha .0125. Augmented therapy minus control: difference 26.74 percentage points (95% CI 7.14–46.35; P = .01). Behavioral minus augmented therapy: 3.91 points (95% CI −15.07 to 22.88; P = .69). Intention-to-treat analysis used multiple imputation for 36/208 missing posttreatment diaries.
results.locator: Full text, Methods: Power Calculation and Statistical Analyses; Results; Table 2

results.measure: Zero episodes on the 7-day bladder diary at 8 weeks
results.note: The report gives a number needed to treat of 10 (95% CI 5.3–44.6) for complete continence.

results.measure: Mean percent reduction from baseline among active-arm participants with 12-month bladder diaries (combined n = 81)
results.note: The delayed-treatment arm was offered treatment after 8 weeks and had no concurrent 12-month comparison.
results.locator: Full text, Methods: Treatment Durability; Results; Table 3

harms.label: Transient hemorrhoidal irritation during electrical stimulation
harms.note: The report identifies these as the two study-related adverse events.

delivery.label: Behavioral program
delivery.value: Four visits approximately 2 weeks apart with a physician investigator or nurse practitioner; pelvic floor contraction taught by anal palpation, three daily exercise sessions of 15 contractions, bladder control strategies, fluid management and diaries.

delivery.label: Augmented program
delivery.value: In-office dual-channel surface EMG feedback and daily home stimulation through an anal probe at 20 Hz, 1-ms pulse width, 5 seconds on/15 seconds off for 15 minutes, up to 100 mA; two daily pelvic floor exercise sessions.
delivery.locator: Full text, Methods: Interventions; PubMed abstract, Interventions

delivery.label: Follow-up and treatment exposure
delivery.value: 176/208 (84.6%) completed the 8-week treatment period; 87/112 (77.7%) active-treatment completers were followed for one year. At 8 weeks, reported adherence to exercises and bladder control strategies was 100% and 93%, respectively, across the active arms.
delivery.locator: Full text, Results, first and final paragraphs
